tips.title: Enable two-factor authentication on email, payment, and social accounts; prioritize phone pop-ups over SMS codes
tips.cost: No cost involved. Each account takes just two to three minutes to set up once.
tips.inPlainWords: Two-factor authentication means an extra verification step beyond the password when logging in. Using a pop-up prompt on your phone that requires a single tap to confirm blocks over 90% of phishing and account theft attempts. In contrast, older verification methods such as answering questions like “Where did you log in last time?” or “What is your backup email?” only block around 10% of such attacks.
tips.benefit: Google analyzed 350,000 real-world account hijacking attempts. For authentication methods relying on device verification — such as phone pop-ups or physical security keys — over 94% of phishing-related hijacking attempts and 100% of automated hijacking attempts were prevented. These automated attempts involve bots using leaked passwords to try logging into accounts in bulk. For verification based on answering personal questions, only 10% of phishing attempts and 73% of automated attempts were blocked.
tips.sources: Doerfler P, Thomas K, Marincenko M, et al. (2019). Evaluating Login Challenges as a Defense Against Account Takeover. The World Wide Web Conference (WWW '19). <https://doi.org/10.1145/3308558.3313481>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The same study also found that these verification methods occasionally block legitimate users from accessing their accounts. 52% of real users failed to log in on their first try. However, 97% of them eventually gained access. It is recommended to enable this feature on email accounts first, as most other accounts allow password recovery via email.

tips.title: Use a unique password solely for your email
tips.cost: No cost involved. Storing it in a password manager eliminates the need to memorize it. The real challenge lies in breaking the old habit of reusing one password across multiple sites.
tips.inPlainWords: If a password you use elsewhere gets stolen, attackers can use it to log straight into your email account. Once they gain access to your email, they can reset passwords for any other accounts linked to it. Therefore, your email password must be unique and never reused anywhere else.
tips.benefit: Credential stuffing is one of the easiest attack methods: attackers simply test stolen passwords against other accounts. If your email password is compromised, all accounts that rely on it for password recovery become vulnerable too. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency recommends using a distinct, strong password of at least 16 characters for every account, and storing it via a password manager.
tips.sources: US CISA. Use Strong Passwords. <https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/use-strong-passwords>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: If you struggle to memorize passwords, use the built-in password manager in your web browser. It stores passwords for each site for you, which is far safer than reusing the same password everywhere. Avoid saving passwords in chat apps, notes or a plain text file.

tips.title: Set a screen lock on your phone and a PIN for the SIM card
tips.cost: No cost at all. You only need to set the screen lock and the SIM PIN once each.
tips.inPlainWords: The SIM card is that tiny card inside your phone that receives SMS verification codes. If your phone gets lost, a finder can remove the card and insert it into another phone to receive those codes, then reset all your accounts one by one. Setting a PIN on the SIM card means that whenever the card is moved to another phone, the user must enter that PIN before the phone can be used — effectively blocking that path.
tips.benefit: Without a SIM PIN, a finder can easily move your SIM card to another phone, receive verification codes, and reset all your accounts. With a PIN in place, that entire process is prevented, keeping your accounts safe even if your phone is lost.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: You can set the SIM PIN under “SIM card lock” in your phone settings. The default factory codes are usually 1234 or 0000. If you enter the wrong code three times in a row, you’ll need the PUK code provided by your carrier to unlock it. After setting the PIN, be sure to write it down somewhere safe.

tips.title: Follow these steps if you lose your phone: block the SIM card, remotely lock it, change passwords, file a police report, and freeze your bank cards if needed.
tips.cost: No cost involved. Completing all steps takes just a few minutes.
tips.inPlainWords: The order of actions matters more than speed. First, block the SIM card to cut off access to verification codes. Next, remotely lock the phone. Then, use a computer to change your email and payment passwords. After that, file a police report to obtain a receipt. Finally, freeze your bank cards as needed. Even if you’re using someone else’s phone, you can still call your carrier to block the SIM card.
tips.benefit: Following the correct sequence is more important than acting quickly. Step one is blocking the SIM card, which severs the main channel for verification codes. Step two involves remotely locking the phone and erasing all its contents. Step three requires changing your email and payment passwords from a computer. Step four is filing a police report to get a receipt. Finally, freeze your bank cards if necessary. The Federal Communications Commission also advises that even if you believe you merely misplaced your phone, you should still remotely lock it. If it’s stolen, file a police report immediately, providing the phone’s model and IMEI number, and inform your carrier right away.
tips.sources: US FCC. Protect Your Smart Device. <https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/protect-your-mobile-device>; The sequence of steps is based on the author’s experience; see section 7 for a replacement ID card, and section 8 about credit information for fake loans.; Department of Telecommunications, Sanchar Saathi. <https://sancharsaathi.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Also note the city where you registered your phone number, as customer service agents will ask for this information. You can still call carrier hotlines from someone else’s phone to block your SIM card.

tips.title: If your card is used fraudulently, report and freeze it first; your liability depends on how fast you report
tips.cost: No cost. Report on the bank's hotline and in writing, then on 1930.
tips.inPlainWords: The RBI's 2017 circular on unauthorised electronic transactions limits your liability if you report at once: zero liability where the fraud is due to a third party and you report within three working days. The bank must credit the amount within 10 working days. Report to the bank and on 1930, and keep the acknowledgement.
tips.benefit: The RBI circular sets a zero-liability rule for a third-party breach reported within three working days, and limited liability for a delay. The bank must resolve the complaint within 90 days. The IT Act and the BNS cover the fraud. A chargeback is separate from the bank's liability. A bank cannot make you pay for its own security failure.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, customer protection circular on unauthorised electronic transactions. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A delay can shift part of the liability to you. Do not share the OTP or PIN, even with a caller who claims to be from the bank. Keep the card blocked until the investigation ends.

tips.title: Periodically check the devices logged into your account and any authorized apps, then remove the ones you no longer use
tips.cost: No cost at all. It only takes a few minutes each time. The hard part is that there’s no reminder — you have to remember to do it yourself.
tips.inPlainWords: “Logged-in devices” refer to the phones and computers that can still access your account right now. Account thieves often lie low for a while before making their move. If you see any unfamiliar devices on the list, or third-party apps you no longer use still linked to your account, log out from all devices and change your password right away.
tips.benefit: Account theft rarely happens instantly — attackers usually spend some time lurking first. The list of logged-in devices shows all phones and computers currently able to access your account, while the list of authorized apps shows all third-party services you’ve given permission to log in using your account. Any unknown devices or unused third-party apps on these lists are the easiest clues to spot.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: This feature exists in Google, Apple and Microsoft accounts, in most banking and UPI apps, and in the security settings of Android and iOS. If you spot any unfamiliar devices, simply log out from all devices and change your password.

tips.title: Don't tap “Allow all” just to use an app: consent must be specific and informed, and you can refuse the permissions the app does not need
tips.cost: No cost involved. The hard part is resisting the urge to tap “Allow all”.
tips.inPlainWords: An app asks for a bundle of permissions at once, and “Allow all” is a single tap that hands over contacts, location, microphone and storage together. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to the personal data necessary for the purpose the app has told you about. A map app can ask for location; a torch app has no business asking for your contacts. You can install the app, refuse the extras, and withdraw consent later as easily as you gave it.
tips.benefit: Section 6(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 defines consent as a free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous agreement, given by a clear affirmative action, to the processing of personal data for a specified purpose, limited to the data necessary for that purpose. Section 5 requires the company to give you notice of the data and the purpose before it asks for consent. Sections 6(4) and 6(5) require withdrawing consent to be as easy as giving it. India's Act does not contain an express right to refuse consent and still receive the service; that protection exists in the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, not here. What you can rely on is purpose limitation, the notice, and the phone's own permission controls.
tips.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, customer protection. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>
tips.caveats: The deciding factor is simple: is this data actually necessary for the service? Location is necessary for a map; a contact list is not necessary for a torch. After installing an app, open the phone's app-permission settings and turn off anything the app does not need; grant a permission when you actually use it, and prefer “only this time” to “while using the app”. If an app will not work unless you hand over data that is plainly unrelated to what it does, that is a reason to use another app, and you can complain to the Data Protection Board of India, which the Act sets up to hear such complaints.

tips.title: You can ask a company to show you, correct and erase your personal data — and complain to the Data Protection Board if it refuses
tips.cost: No cost to make the request. If the company drags its feet, the next step is a complaint to the Data Protection Board of India, which is free; a civil suit for damages is a separate, slow and expensive route.
tips.inPlainWords: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 you can ask a company what personal data it holds about you and get a summary, ask for correction or erasure, complain about how it handled your data, and nominate someone to exercise these rights if you die or become incapacitated. Deactivating an account and erasing the data are two separate actions, so after you close the account, ask for erasure separately. If the company refuses or ignores you, you can complain to the Data Protection Board of India.
tips.benefit: The Act gives four rights. Section 11 lets you ask for a summary of the personal data a Data Fiduciary holds about you, the identity of the fiduciaries it has shared it with, and a description of the data. Section 12 gives you correction, completion and updating, and erasure where the purpose has been served and there is no legal duty to keep it. Section 13 gives you a grievance-redressal route, and the company must answer. Section 14 lets you nominate someone to exercise your rights if you die or become incapacitated. The Data Protection Board of India, set up under section 18, hears complaints and can impose penalties.
tips.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Direction. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>
tips.caveats: The right to erasure stops where another law requires retention: a bank keeps KYC records under the RBI's master directions, a company keeps tax and company-law records, and an investigation can put a hold on data. Deactivating an account is not the same as erasing the data, so ask for both, in writing. Before you switch phones or sell a device, log out of every account, unlink them and factory-reset the handset. The Act gives you a complaint route and penalties, not compensation; a claim for money would need a separate civil suit. The law cannot retrieve data that has already leaked.

tips.title: You are not obliged to use facial recognition: ask for a password, an OTP, a card or an in-person check instead
tips.cost: No cost involved. When you are asked for a face scan, ask what other verification methods are available. The challenge is voicing the question on the spot.
tips.inPlainWords: A face scan is convenient, but it is rarely the only way to prove who you are. India has no facial-recognition-specific statute of the kind that would stop a private operator from making it the only option. What India does have is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which covers biometric data like any other personal data: it needs your free, specific, informed consent, a notice of the purpose, and no more data than the purpose requires. So you can decline, ask for an alternative, and withdraw consent later.
tips.benefit: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has no special regime for faces; the same rules apply to biometric data. Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to what is necessary (section 6). The company must give you notice of what it will collect and why (section 5), and must let you withdraw consent as easily as you gave it. For a government body, Aadhaar authentication is voluntary: the Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018) held that Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for a service without legal backing, and the Aadhaar Act, 2016 requires consent and provides for alternative means of identification. For banks, the RBI's KYC Master Direction recognises video-based customer identification with the customer's consent, alongside branch and other modes.
tips.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Aadhaar Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Unique Identification Authority of India. <https://uidai.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Direction. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Common requests come from apartment gates, gyms, hotels and rental platforms. When you are told “the system only does face recognition”, ask for the alternative and put the request in writing; a card, a PIN, an OTP or a photo-ID check usually exists. India has no rule that bans cameras in changing rooms, but filming a person in a private space without consent is the offence of voyeurism under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the data protection Act applies to whatever is captured. Financial and government services may have their own rules. Unlike a password, a face cannot be changed after a leak, so it deserves more caution. Your rights to see and erase the data are covered in item 8.

tips.title: Do not entrust proprietary code, API keys, or confidential data to unverified "AI relay proxy stations," especially when allowing AI agents to execute local commands autonomously
tips.cost: Direct official API access is typically more expensive than third-party relay proxies, and recharging balances can be less convenient. The friction lies in the temptation: relay proxies are cheap and provide access to multiple foundational models through a single endpoint.
tips.inPlainWords: An intermediary proxy sits directly between you and the model provider: it can observe, intercept, and modify everything you send and receive. In an empirical study evaluating over 400 proxy stations, 9 injected malicious code into model responses, and 17 actively hijacked intentionally seeded cloud service credentials. If you allow AI agents to execute commands locally on your machine, a single tampered command is enough to compromise full system control.
tips.benefit: CERT-In is India's national agency for cyber incidents, and the practical warning is the same: an unverified third-party proxy relay retains submitted user data on remote servers, intercepts proprietary code, or resells private datasets to other model providers for training. Some proxies conceal backdoors, injecting malicious payloads into user devices to harvest credentials and install remote administration trojans. Use direct official API connections or officially licensed platforms, and avoid unlicensed, unverified proxies. Sensitive data and project documentation should be sanitized and desensitized before transmission, and API keys must be rotated regularly. If abnormal billing, unexplained bans, or data anomalies occur, discontinue service immediately, revoke keys, scan for malware, and preserve evidence. A 2026 empirical study by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and collaborator institutions evaluated 28 commercial relay services purchased across online storefronts and 400 public free proxies. Results showed that 1 paid service and 8 free proxies injected malicious code into returned tool-call outputs (system commands instructed by the AI to run on local machines, such as package installations). Furthermore, 2 services strategically timed their attacks, selectively targeting fully autonomous agent execution sessions. Seventeen proxies actively abused intentionally placed Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials, and 1 drained test funds from an Ethereum test wallet (loss under $50). The study demonstrated subtle, stealthy tampering techniques: for instance, replacing standard packages like `requests` with typosquatted dependencies like `reqeusts` in command payloads, which easily escapes visual inspection.
tips.sources: Liu H, Shou C, Wen H, Chen Y, Fang RJ, Feng Y. (2026). Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain. arXiv:2604.08407. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08407>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Rated Grade B because it relies on a single empirical preprint prior to peer-reviewed publication. The majority of evaluated relays were free public endpoints, with only 28 commercial services tested, precluding an exact statistical percentage of compromised market share. Some media reports mistakenly exaggerated the test wallet theft to $500,000; the actual loss reported in the paper was under $50. Benefit is rated medium due to the severity of credential leaks and device takeover risks, though individual financial losses vary. If you have previously routed sensitive requests through unknown proxies, immediately revoke and regenerate affected API keys with the official model provider, as well as any exposed cloud provider and code repository access tokens. When routing through third-party proxies, never grant AI agents unreviewed autonomous command execution—manually inspect every shell command before confirmation. For criminal liabilities associated with operating unauthorized proxy relays, see Chapter 11, Rule 19.

tips.title: Audit the SIM cards and bank accounts linked to your identity once a year
tips.cost: No cost. The TAFCOP check is free, and the annual credit report is free.
tips.inPlainWords: India limits the number of SIM cards a person may hold. Use the Sanchar Saathi or TAFCOP portal to see the mobile connections in your name and report an unknown one. Check your credit report for a loan or card you did not apply for, and close an unused account. An unknown SIM can be used for OTP fraud.
tips.benefit: The Department of Telecommunications' TAFCOP lets you check the mobile connections issued against your ID and report the unauthorised ones. The RBI's KYC rules require the bank to verify the customer. A credit bureau report shows a loan or card in your name. The Aadhaar Act restricts the use of Aadhaar. The BNS and the IT Act cover identity theft.
tips.sources: Department of Telecommunications, Sanchar Saathi. <https://sancharsaathi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; TransUnion CIBIL. <https://www.cibil.com/>; Aadhaar Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A family member may have used your ID for a SIM; ask before reporting. A closed account can still show for a month. Do not share an OTP with anyone who offers to 'check' your SIM.

tips.title: Before you give up a mobile number, move every account off it — and port the number instead if you can
tips.cost: No cost apart from the operator's porting charge. Migrating accounts takes an hour or two, and updating the number registered with your bank is done in the banking app or at the branch. The difficulty is remembering the rarely used services.
tips.inPlainWords: A disconnected mobile number goes back into the operator's pool and is eventually allotted to someone else. Any account still linked to that number can then be unlocked with a one-time password sent by SMS to the new owner. So before you surrender a number, move your bank, UPI, email, social and government accounts to the new number; India has no single “unbind everything” service, so this is done provider by provider. If you are only changing operator or circle, port the number instead, under mobile number portability, and keep every linkage intact.
tips.benefit: India's mobile number portability regime, run under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's portability regulations, lets you keep the number when you change operator or circle, which avoids the problem entirely for most people. The Department of Telecommunications' Sanchar Saathi portal lets you see the connections issued in your name and report one you do not recognise. There is no Indian equivalent of the single national unbinding service that some countries run: each bank, wallet, email provider and social platform has its own change-of-number or account-closure route, and the RBI's KYC master directions require your bank to keep the registered mobile number current. Do the accounts that can move money first.
tips.sources: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, mobile number portability. <https://www.trai.gov.in/>; Department of Telecommunications, Sanchar Saathi. <https://sancharsaathi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Direction. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Start with the accounts that can move money — bank, UPI, cards, demat, insurance — and only then the social and shopping accounts. Keep the old number alive on the cheapest plan for one to two months so that a forgotten verification code still reaches you, and forward calls if the operator allows it. Check the connections in your name on Sanchar Saathi before you close anything. If a number is already disconnected, the operator cannot recover the SMS and you will have to prove your identity to each provider another way, which is slow. Managing unauthorised device logins is covered in Chapter 14, Rule 6; wiping an old phone before selling it is covered in Rule 8.
